title: Module Documentation: Totient Iteration to Primes
content: Erdős Problem #409: how many iterations of $n \mapsto \varphi(n) + 1$ reach a prime? The sequence is strictly decreasing for composite $n$ (since $\varphi(n) + 1 < n$), so always terminates at a prime. $F(n)$ counts the iterations needed. Key questions: can infinitely many $n$ reach the same prime? What density of $n$ reaches a fixed prime? $F(n) = o(n)$ is trivial; $F(n) = 1$ infinitely often (when $\varphi(n) + 1$ is prime). A problem of Finucane, popularized by Erdős and Graham (1980, p. 81). OEIS A039651.
mathContext: Define $f(n) = \varphi(n) + 1$ and $F(n) = \min\{k : f^{(k)}(n) \text{ is prime}\}$. Since $\varphi(n) + 1 < n$ for composite $n > 1$, the iteration terminates.

title: Totient Decrease and Iteration Termination Proofs
content: The core proved results establishing that the iteration terminates. `iterate_decreasing`: for composite $n > 1$, $\varphi(n) + 1 < n$. Proof: $\varphi(n) \leq n - 2$ for composite $n$ because both 0 and $\min\text{Fac}(n)$ are not coprime to $n$, so at least 2 elements of $[0, n)$ are excluded from the totient count. Uses `Finset.card_le_card` after showing the coprime filter misses at least $\{0, \min\text{Fac}(n)\}$. The `iteration_terminates` theorem then proves the iteration reaches a prime, using well-founded recursion on $\mathbb{N}$.
mathContext: $\varphi(n) = |\{k \in [0,n) : \gcd(k,n) = 1\}|$. For composite $n$: $0$ and $\min\text{Fac}(n)$ are not coprime to $n$, so $\varphi(n) \leq n - 2$, hence $\varphi(n) + 1 \leq n - 1 < n$.

title: Iteration Count and Basic Properties
content: Defines `iterationsToFirst` counting how many steps to reach a prime, and proves basic properties. For primes, $F(p) = 0$ (already prime). For composite $n$, $F(n) = F(\varphi(n)+1) + 1$ (one more step than the successor). Uses `Nat.strongRecOn` for the well-founded definition and `sSup` for the supremum characterization.
mathContext: $F(p) = 0$ for prime $p$. $F(n) = 1 + F(\varphi(n)+1)$ for composite $n > 1$. The function is well-defined by the decreasing chain $n > \varphi(n) + 1 > \cdots$.

title: Sigma Variant and Open Conjectures
content: The closing section explores the variant using the sum-of-divisors function $\sigma(n)$ instead of $\varphi(n)$. Proves `sigma_growing`, `sigma_prime_fixed`, and `sigma_composite_growth`: this iteration is non-decreasing at composites ($\sigma(n) - 1 \geq n$, in fact $\geq n + 1$) and fixed at primes ($\sigma(p) - 1 = p$), a fundamentally different dynamical system from the $\varphi$-iteration. States the open conjectures about density of $n$ reaching specific primes, finiteness of the iteration for all $n$, and the relationship between the $\varphi$ and $\sigma$ variants.
mathContext: Variant: $g(n) = \sigma(n) - 1$ (sum of divisors minus one). Unlike the $\varphi$-iteration, $g$ is non-decreasing for composites ($\sigma(n) - 1 \geq n$) and fixed at primes, so termination at a prime is not guaranteed. Open: characterize which primes are reachable.

title: Imports and Dependencies
content: Imports Mathlib's Euler totient function ($\texttt{Nat.totient}$), primality definitions, and the filter framework for expressing asymptotic bounds like $F(n) = o(n)$.
mathContext: Requires $\varphi(n) = |\{1 \leq k \leq n : \gcd(k,n) = 1\}|$, $\texttt{Nat.Prime}$, and the $\texttt{atTop}$ filter for $o(\cdot)$ notation.

title: Totient-Plus-One Map
content: The dynamical map $T(n) = \varphi(n) + 1$. For composite $n > 1$, $\varphi(n) < n - 1$ (since at least $n$ and 1 are not coprime to $n$), so $T(n) \leq n - 1 < n$, making the map strictly decreasing on composites. For primes $p$, $\varphi(p) + 1 = (p-1) + 1 = p$, so primes are fixed points. This defines a discrete dynamical system on $\mathbb{N}$ whose orbits descend to primes.
mathContext: $T(n) = \varphi(n) + 1$. For composite $n$: $T(n) < n$. For prime $p$: $T(p) = p$.

title: Iterated Totient-Plus-One
content: The $k$-th iterate $T^k(n) = T(T(\cdots T(n)\cdots))$ using Lean's $\texttt{Nat.iterate}$. The orbit $n, T(n), T^2(n), \ldots$ forms a strictly decreasing sequence until a prime is reached.
mathContext: $T^k(n) = \underbrace{T \circ T \circ \cdots \circ T}_{k}(n)$. The orbit is $n > T(n) > T^2(n) > \cdots > T^{F(n)}(n) = p$ (prime).

title: $F(n)$ — Iteration Count to First Prime
content: The minimum number of applications of $T(n) = \varphi(n) + 1$ needed to reach a prime, starting from $n$. For primes, $F(p) = 0$. The definition uses $\texttt{sSup}$ to find the first $k$ where $T^k(n)$ is prime. OEIS A039651 lists the first values of $F(n)$.
mathContext: $F(n) = \min\{k \geq 0 : T^k(n) \text{ is prime}\}$. First values: $F(2)=0, F(3)=0, F(4)=1, F(5)=0, F(6)=1, F(7)=0, F(8)=2, \ldots$

title: Termination Guarantee
content: For any $n > 0$, the iteration reaches a prime. The proof is elementary: since $\varphi(n) + 1 < n$ for composite $n > 1$, the orbit $n, T(n), T^2(n), \ldots$ is a strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers, which must terminate at a prime (every positive integer $> 1$ is either prime or has a smaller value under $T$).
mathContext: $\forall n > 0,\; \exists k,\; T^k(n) \text{ is prime}$. Proof: the sequence $(T^j(n))_j$ is eventually decreasing and bounded below by 2.

title: Strict Decrease for Composites
content: For composite $n > 1$, $\varphi(n) + 1 < n$. This follows from $\varphi(n) \leq n - \sqrt{n}$ for composites (since $n$ has a prime factor $p \leq \sqrt{n}$, and at least $n/p$ multiples of $p$ are not coprime to $n$). The strict decrease ensures the orbit descends.
mathContext: $n > 1,\; n \text{ composite} \Rightarrow \varphi(n) + 1 < n$. In fact $\varphi(n) \leq n(1 - 1/p)$ for any prime $p \mid n$.

title: Part (i): $F(n) = o(n)$
content: The trivial bound: $F(n) = o(n)$ since each iteration reduces $n$ by at least 1 (for composites). Cambie observed this is easy; the real question is whether $F(n) = O(\log n)$ or $F(n) = O(\log \log n)$. Since $\varphi(n) \approx n/e^\gamma \cdot \prod_{p|n}(1-1/p)$, each step typically reduces $n$ by a constant factor, suggesting $F(n) = O(\log n)$.
mathContext: $F(n) = o(n)$ as $n \to \infty$. Heuristically, $F(n) = O(\log n)$ since $\varphi(n)/n$ has average value $6/\pi^2 \approx 0.608$.

title: Part (ii): Infinitely Many to Same Prime
content: Can infinitely many starting values $n$ reach the same prime $p$ under iteration of $T$? The set $\{n : \exists k,\; T^k(n) = p\}$ is the 'basin of attraction' of $p$. For $p = 2$, this includes all even composites and many odd values. The question is whether any prime has an infinite basin — which seems likely for small primes like 2 and 3.
mathContext: $\exists p \text{ prime},\; |\{n \in \mathbb{N} : \exists k,\; T^k(n) = p\}| = \infty$?

title: Part (iii): Density of Basin
content: For each prime $p$, does the set $\{n : \exists k,\; T^k(n) = p\}$ have a natural density? If so, what is it? The density measures the 'probability' that a random large integer eventually reaches $p$ under the totient-plus-one iteration. Understanding these densities would give a complete picture of the global dynamics of $T$.
mathContext: $\alpha(p) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{|\{n \leq N : \exists k,\; T^k(n) = p\}|}{N}$ exists?

title: $F(p) = 0$ for Primes
content: Primes are already at the target: $F(p) = 0$ since $T^0(p) = p$ is prime. This is the base case for the iteration.
mathContext: $p$ prime $\Rightarrow F(p) = 0$.

title: $F(n) = 1$ Criterion
content: $F(n) = 1$ when $\varphi(n) + 1$ is prime. This happens for $n = 4$ ($\varphi(4)+1 = 3$), $n = 6$ ($\varphi(6)+1 = 3$), $n = 8$ ($\varphi(8)+1 = 5$), $n = 12$ ($\varphi(12)+1 = 5$), etc. The set of such $n$ is infinite (related to Goldbach-type questions about which primes are of the form $\varphi(n) + 1$).
mathContext: $F(n) = 1 \iff \varphi(n) + 1$ is prime. Examples: $n \in \{4, 6, 8, 12, 14, 18, 20, \ldots\}$.

title: $\varphi(n) + 1$ is Odd for $n \geq 3$
content: For $n \geq 3$, $\varphi(n)$ is even (a well-known property: if $n$ has an odd prime factor $p$, then $p-1 \mid \varphi(n)$; if $n = 2^k$ with $k \geq 2$, then $\varphi(n) = 2^{k-1}$ is even). Thus $\varphi(n) + 1$ is odd, making it a candidate for odd primality. This means the orbit enters the odd integers after at most one step.
mathContext: $n \geq 3 \Rightarrow 2 \mid \varphi(n) \Rightarrow \varphi(n) + 1$ is odd.

title: Sigma Variant: $n \mapsto \sigma(n) - 1$
content: The companion problem using the sum-of-divisors function: iterate $n \mapsto \sigma(n) - 1$. Unlike the totient variant, $\sigma(n) \geq n + 1$ for composite $n$ (since $1, n \in$ divisors), so $\sigma(n) - 1 \geq n$. The sequence is non-decreasing for composites, making termination at a prime uncertain. This fundamentally different dynamical behavior — growth vs descent — makes the sigma variant a separate open question.
mathContext: $\sigma(n) - 1 \geq n$ for composite $n$, so the orbit may diverge. Contrast: $\varphi(n) + 1 < n$ for composites.

title: Sigma Iteration Grows
content: For composite $n > 1$, $\sigma(n) - 1 \geq n$ since $\sigma(n) \geq 1 + n$ (the divisors include at least 1 and $n$ itself, plus others for composites). This makes the sigma variant grow rather than shrink, with no guarantee of reaching a prime.
mathContext: $n$ composite $\Rightarrow \sigma(n) \geq 1 + d + n > n + 1$ for some divisor $d > 1$, so $\sigma(n) - 1 > n$.

title: Fixed Point: $\varphi(2) + 1 = 2$
content: The prime 2 is a fixed point of the totient-plus-one map: $\varphi(2) + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2$. This is the unique even fixed point. All orbits that pass through an even composite will eventually reach 2 (since 2 is the only even prime). Proved directly by $\texttt{simp}$.
mathContext: $T(2) = \varphi(2) + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2$. The only even prime is a fixed point.

title: $F(n) = 1$ Infinitely Often
content: The set $\{n > 1 : \varphi(n) + 1 \text{ is prime}\}$ is infinite. This follows because there are infinitely many $n$ with $\varphi(n) = p - 1$ for some prime $p$ (e.g., $n = 2(p-1)$ gives $\varphi(n) = p - 1$ when $p - 1$ is even, which is always for $p > 2$). The result shows the iteration frequently terminates in a single step.
mathContext: $|\{n > 1 : \varphi(n) + 1 \text{ is prime}\}| = \infty$.
